advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Filter the Windows descendant walk by process creation time (child created at or after parent) so stale parent-pid entries left by pid reuse are never terminated
evidence: _descendants builds the tree from pid/parent pairs only: `for pid, parent in table: if pid != parent: children.setdefault(parent, []).append(pid)`
_windows_process_table records only `(int(entry.th32ProcessID), int(entry.th32ParentProcessID))`, with no creation time

The comment's premise only covers reuse AFTER spawn: 'the caller's un-waited Popen keeps the child's handle open so its pid cannot be reused' — it does not exclude a pre-existing process that already names the recycled pid as its parent, and intermediate descendant pids are not held at all
src/rebar/_proc.py:38 `_kill_windows_descendants(proc.pid, label=label, logger=logger)` terminates every pid the walk returns

The diff's own test comment acknowledges the hazard: 'On a Windows host the real descendant walk would end whatever runner processes name that pid as their parent' (tests/unit/reconciler/state/test_acli_subprocess_timeout.py)
advisory.finding: The Windows descendant walk treats any process whose th32ParentProcessID equals the child's (or a descendant's) pid as a descendant, without checking that it was created after that parent. Windows recycles pids and does not clear stale parent-pid fields, so an unrelated, long-orphaned process whose dead parent's pid was later reused for the timed-out child (e.g. explorer.exe, whose parent pid points at an exited userinit.exe) will be TerminateProcess'd.
scenarios: A grounding/ACLI child times out on Windows after being given a recycled pid that a still-running orphan (explorer.exe, a service host child, another user tool) names as its parent; the reaper kills that unrelated process
advisory.suggested_fix: Record each process's creation time in the table (OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION) + GetProcessTimes) and accept an entry as a child of `parent` only when child_creation >= parent_creation, as psutil/Chromium do. Add a fake-table unit test with a process that predates the root.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the Windows descendant walk confirm each process's identity before ending it: require a child to have started after its listed parent, and open a handle and check that same handle before calling TerminateProcess.
evidence: Shared mutable resource: the host's Windows process/PID table, read through `snap = k32.CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(_TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS, 0)` (src/rebar/_proc.py:126) and `table.append((int(entry.th32ProcessID), int(entry.th32ParentProcessID)))` (src/rebar/_proc.py:135).

Executor 1: the reaper. reap_process_group calls `_kill_windows_descendants(proc.pid, label=label, logger=logger)` (src/rebar/_proc.py:38). It is reached from src/rebar/_store/gitutil.py:311, src/rebar/grounding/harness.py:121, src/rebar/reconciler/adapters/jira/acli_subprocess.py:476, src/rebar/_bridge_runner.py:156 and src/rebar/reconciler/adapters/jira_family/wiki_render.py:397.

Executor 2: every other process on the host, which creates and exits processes and so causes PIDs to be reused while the reaper runs. Inside this tree, the second pass at src/rebar/_proc.py:191 (`for _ in range(_DESCENDANT_PASSES)`) exists because descendants can start processes between snapshots.

Window A, PID checked once and used later: the read `found = _descendants(root, _windows_process_table())` (src/rebar/_proc.py:193) and the later write `handle = k32.OpenProcess(_PROCESS_TERMINATE, False, pid)` / `k32.TerminateProcess(handle, 1)` (src/rebar/_proc.py:154, :158). If a listed descendant exits and its PID is reused in between, the new unrelated process is the one terminated. No process creation time or held handle ties the PID to the process the snapshot saw.

Window B, stale parent PID: `children.setdefault(parent, []).append(pid)` (src/rebar/_proc.py:172) treats every entry's stored parent PID as current. A long-lived unrelated process whose real parent exited keeps that dead PID as its parent PID. If the dead PID was later given to one of our descendants, the unrelated process appears in the tree and gets terminated. The comment at src/rebar/_proc.py:87-90 only argues against reuse of the root PID (`the caller's un-waited Popen keeps the child's handle open so its pid cannot be reused`). No handle is held for intermediate PIDs, so that argument does not cover them.

Guard absence: the except at src/rebar/_proc.py:202 (`except OSError as exc:  # already gone, or not ours to end`) only handles the case where termination fails. When the PID has been reused by a process the same user can open, the call succeeds and kills that process.
advisory.finding: On Windows, _kill_windows_descendants can terminate a process that is not a descendant. It builds the tree from parent-PID values in a Toolhelp snapshot and later calls OpenProcess/TerminateProcess by bare PID. Nothing confirms the process at that PID is the one the snapshot saw. Nothing confirms a listed parent PID still refers to the original parent, because Windows does not keep a parent PID current after the parent exits and the PID is reused. Only the root's PID is protected from reuse.
scenarios: A git op or acli/grounding tool times out on a Windows workstation. A grandchild exits during the snapshot-to-terminate window, and the user's editor, shell or another rebar process takes its PID before OpenProcess runs. That process is terminated.

A long-lived process such as explorer.exe still lists an exited launcher's PID as its parent. That PID has since been reused by the timed-out child's grandchild, so the walk counts the long-lived process as a descendant and terminates it.
advisory.suggested_fix: Record each process's creation time (OpenProcess with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION | PROCESS_TERMINATE plus GetProcessTimes) and count an entry as a child only if it was created after its listed parent. Then call TerminateProcess on the same handle used for the identity check rather than reopening by PID. Better still, launch the child in a Job Object with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE and use TerminateJobObject, which avoids walking by PID altogether.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Port test_fetch_coordination_lock_serializes_on_shared_common_dir (and the wedged-peer degrade test) to lock_kernel.take_exclusive / take_blocking_exclusive, and drop the module-level importorskip("fcntl") so they run on Windows
evidence: tests/unit/test_fetch_common_dir_coordination.py:23: `fcntl = pytest.importorskip("fcntl")` — module-level skip on Windows

tests/unit/test_fetch_common_dir_coordination.py:116-117: `with pytest.raises(OSError):
    fcntl.flock(fd, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)` — the serialization check is written against fcntl directly
tests/unit/test_fetch_common_dir_coordination.py:311: `fcntl.flock(holder, fcntl.LOCK_EX)` — the wedged-peer degrade test also holds via fcntl
Diff adds to src/rebar/_store/git_locking.py `_acquire_fetch_coord_flock`: `lock_kernel.take_exclusive(fd)` and to fetch_coordination_lock release: `lock_kernel.release_exclusive(fd)`
tests/unit/store/test_git_locking_no_fcntl.py only covers the no-leg-at-all path (both fcntl and msvcrt patched to None), not the msvcrt-present leg
advisory.finding: The diff moves fetch_coordination_lock / _acquire_fetch_coord_flock onto lock_kernel.take_exclusive so that it really locks on Windows. But every test that checks this lock actually excludes a peer lives in a module that is skipped wherever fcntl is absent. So the new msvcrt leg of the fetch lock never runs in the Windows sweep. The git-op lock gets a Windows contention test; the fetch lock does not.
scenarios: On Windows: hold fetch_coordination_lock(main) while a peer opens rebar-fetch.lock in the shared common dir and calls lock_kernel.take_exclusive on its own fd. That should raise OSError, but no Windows test checks it.
A broken msvcrt release (for example the lseek anchor missing) would leave the second acquirer blocked until the wait budget runs out, and nothing on Windows would catch it.
advisory.suggested_fix: Replace the direct fcntl.flock calls in test_fetch_common_dir_coordination.py with lock_kernel.take_exclusive(fd) / lock_kernel.release_exclusive(fd) / lock_kernel.take_blocking_exclusive(holder). Remove the module-level `pytest.importorskip("fcntl")`, or narrow it to the specific tests that still need it.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a fake-table test where terminating one descendant adds a new child row, and assert the second pass ends it too
evidence:
Diff adds to src/rebar/_proc.py: `#: Walk passes: the second catches a process a descendant started while the first ran.
_DESCENDANT_PASSES = 2`
tests/unit/test_proc_reap_windows.py `_force_windows.terminate` only removes rows: `table[:] = [row for row in table if row[0] != pid]`, so no new descendant ever appears between passes
test_the_windows_reap_kills_the_child_then_its_descendants asserts `ended == [5001, 5000]`, which is the same with one pass or two
advisory.finding: _kill_windows_descendants makes a second walk pass (_DESCENDANT_PASSES = 2) to catch a process that a descendant started while the first pass ran. No test drives that path. In every fake-table test the second pass either finds nothing (the table shrinks as pids end) or finds the same pids again (terminate fails). Removing the second pass, or breaking its loop, would leave all tests green.
scenarios: A fake terminate that, on ending pid 5000, appends (5002, 4321) to the table. The current code should also end 5002 on pass 2, but no test asserts it.
advisory.suggested_fix: In test_proc_reap_windows.py, add a test whose fake terminate(pid) appends (7000, 4321) the first time it is called with 5000. Then assert 7000 is in `ended` after reap_process_group.
